Synthesis of fluoride
The FeO0.7F1.3 was prepared by a facile thermal treatment of hydrate iron fluoride, which was obtained based on a dissolution-precipitation method in an ionic liquid medium25. Firstly, a certain amount of Ketjen Black (KB, Shenzhen Kejing Zhida Technology Co., Ltd., 25 wt% in the final weight of fluoride composite) was added into 10 mL of ionic liquid 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate (BmimBF4, Aladdin, 98%), followed by vigorous stirring at 50 °C for several hours to form a uniform black solution. Then, it was transferred into the ice-water bath and cooled down to 0 °C, and 1.0 g of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (Aladdin, 98%) was gradually added into the KB-suspended solution under stirring state. The reaction solution was kept stirred for 12 h at the ice-water bath to allow sufficient fluorination. The precipitate product (FeF3·3H2O/KB) was washed with acetone (Adamas, 99.9%) and centrifuged several times, followed by drying under vacuum at 80 °C for 12 h. Finally, the hydrate iron fluoride composite was heated at 300 °C for 5 h with a ramping rate of 5 °C min−1 to obtain the FeO0.7F1.3 sample. The as-prepared FeO0.7F1.3 sample contains a dominant phase of FeO0.77F1.23 and a minor phase of FeF3 at the molar percentages of 85.51% and 14.49%, respectively25.

Electrolyte preparation
AlCl3 (>98.0%) and tris(pentafluorophenyl)borane (TPFPB, >98.0%) were bought from Tokyo Chemical Industry Co. Ltd. Tetrahydrofuran (THF, ≥99.8%) was acquired from Alfa Aesar. Phenylmagnesium chloride (PhMgCl, ≥99.8%) and LiCl (≥99.99%) were purchased from Aladdin Reagent Co. The baseline all phenyl complex (APC)-type electrolyte was synthesized by reacting 0.25 M AlCl3 and 0.5 M PhMgCl and adding 1.0 M LiCl in THF. Specifically, 0.1333 g of AlCl3 was dissolved in 3 mL of THF with stirring overnight, and then 1 mL PhMgCl (2.0 M in THF) was added into the above solution. After the sufficient Lewis acid-base reactions, 0.1696 g LiCl was added into the solution and continuously stirred until it was completely dissolved prior to use (denoted as LiCl-APC). The additive-containing electrolyte was obtained by dissolving 0.02 M or 0.05 M TPFPB into the above LiCl-APC solution. Among them, the optimal formulation with 0.02 M TPFPB is denoted as LiCl-APC-TPFPB and used for a comparative study with the baseline LiCl-APC. All the electrolytes were prepared inside an Ar-filled glove box with oxygen and moisture contents lower than 0.1 ppm at a room temperature of 25 °C.

Electrochemical measurement
The electrochemical performance was investigated by using CR2032 coin-type cells with the as-synthesized oxyfluoride as positive electrode and the high-purity magnesium foil (Hefei KE JING Materials Technology Co., LTD., 99.95%, 50 μm in thickness) as negative electrode. The positive electrode was prepared by homogeneously mixing the FeO0.7F1.3 powder, Super P carbon (Shenzhen Kejing Zhida Technology Co., Ltd.) and poly(vinyldifluoride) (PVDF, Sigma Aldrich, Mw = ~534,000) binder with a weight ratio of 8:1:1 in the N-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., AR) solvent, followed by pasting the slurry on the 8-mm-diameter carbon paper (Toray, TGP-H-060, which was attached on a Mo current collector) and drying in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 20 h to remove the solvent. The prepared positive electrode contains the active fluoride material with a mass loading of about 1.0 mg cm−2 and has a thickness of about 24 μm. The negative-to-positive electrode capacity ratio (N/P ratio) is estimated to be about 63.6. A glass microfiber membrane (Whatman GF/B, cat. No. 1821-090, thickness=0.68 mm, average pore size=1.0 μm) with a diameter of 19 mm was employed as the separator. The APC-type solutions with and without TPFPB additive were used as the electrolytes. The volume of electrolyte injected in each coin cell is controlled at about 90 μl by pipette. The whole cell assembly process was carried out in an Ar-filled glove box.

Regular galvanostatic charge-discharge tests were operated at room temperature (25 °C, if not specially indicated) on a LAND-CT2001A battery system at various specific currents from 100 to 1000 mA g-1. The charge cut-off potential is set at 2.5, 2.7, or 3.0 V vs. Mg2+/Mg. The discharge cut-off potential is set at 1.1 V for intercalation reaction or at 0.5 V for additional conversion reaction. The cell for low temperature test was pre-cycled at 25 °C for 5 cycles and then transferred to an environment of –20 °C to conduct the following electrochemical cycling at a specific current of 20 mA g−1 in a voltage range of 0.5-3.0 V. GITT was operated at 25 °C and a low specific current of 20 mA g−1 for 1 h followed by open-circuit relaxation for 6 h to reach a quasi-equilibrium state. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), Tafel analysis, and in-situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were performed on an electrochemical workstation (VersaSTAT3, AMETEK Scientific Instruments) at 25 °C. CV measurements of Mg||FeO0.7F1.3 cells were run at different scan rates from 0.1 to 1.0 mV s−1 in various voltage ranges of 0.5–2.5 V, 0.5–2.7 V, and 0.5–3.0 V. To evaluate the oxidation stability of APC-type electrolytes and their anodic corrosion on metallic current collectors, LSV tests were conducted at a scan rate of 0.1 mV s−1 using a two-electrode or three-electrode configuration. Stainless steel (SS) or Mo foil was used as the working electrode, and Mg foils serve as the counter electrode for two-electrode configuration and as both the reference electrode and counter electrode for three-electrode configuration, respectively. The reversibility of Mg plating/stripping process in APC-type electrolytes was evaluated by conducting the galvanostatic cycling in Mg||Cu asymmetric cells at a current density of 0.5 mA cm−2 and an areal capacity of 1.0 mAh cm−2. The Cu foil (99.9%) with a thickness of 12 μm was acquired from Hefei KE JING Materials Technology Co., LTD. Tafel analysis was performed on the 10th discharge process by holding the voltage at the conversion plateau of 1.20 V for 1 h, followed by a linear scan at 1.0 mV s−1 within the voltage range of ±100 mV around the open-circuit voltage. For in-situ EIS measurements, the Mg||FeO0.7F1.3 cell was pre-cycled for 10 cycles at 100 mA g−1 in a voltage range of 0.5–3.0 V to allow the electrodes and related interfaces to reach a quasi-stable state. Then, the cell intermittently proceeded with a galvanostatic discharge-charge cycle at 100 mA g−1 in a voltage range of 0.5–3.0 V, with a specific capacity interval of 35 mAh g−1, followed by an open-circuit operation for 30 min and a potentiostatic EIS measurement to record the Nyquist plots. Each potentiostatic EIS measurement was conducted under the open-circuit condition with an applied amplitude of 10 mV, in a frequency range from 100 kHz to 1.0 Hz (12 points per decade). The obtained Nyquist plots are deconvolved for the DRT analysis using pyDRTtools software58.

Material characterization
Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy were performed to identify the effect of TPFPB mediation on the composition and solvation structure of APC-type electrolytes. The 11B and 7Li NMR spectra were collected on a Bruker Avance III HD 400 MHz spectrometer. Raman spectra were measured with a Renishaw inVia Reflex confocal Raman microscope using a 633 nm laser. The ionic conductivities of baseline APC-type electrolyte and TPFPB-containing electrolyte were measured by a DDSJ-308A conductivity meter (Leici) at 25 °C. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Magellan 400L, FEI) was employed to observe the morphology of pristine FeO0.7F1.3 grains. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL JSM-6700F, operated at 200 kV) was carried out to collect the (high-resolution) TEM images and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns, which are used to disclose the morphology and microstructure of oxyfluoride positive electrodes at terminal discharged and charged states. The (sub)surface composition and bonding evolutions of cycled FeO0.7F1.3 electrodes were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCAlab-250) with an Al anode source. For the ex-situ TEM and XPS characterizations, the discharged or charged FeO0.7F1.3 electrode was cycled at 100 mA g−1 and 25 °C for 5 cycles, and then taken out from the cells in an Ar-filled glove box. Subsequently, the collected electrodes were repeatedly washed by THF solvent to ensure the removal of residual salts. They were then dried overnight in an argon atmosphere before further characterization.

Computational details
Quantum chemical calculations were carried out using the Gaussian 09 (Revision D.01)59 software package based on density functional theory (DFT) method. The geometry optimization and single-point energy calculation were performed at the B3LYP60/6-311+G(d,p)61//M062X62/def2TZVP63 level of theory. The electrostatic potential (ESP) mapping of molecular surface with ESP surface extrema was obtained using Multiwfn (version 3.8) software64 and Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD, version 1.9.4a53) program65 based on the above single-point energy calculation. Supplementary Data 1-6 provide the optimized configurations of THF solvent and Cl− and AlCl4− anions individually, as well as their respective optimized configurations when interacting with TPFPB. The desolvation energy profiles of solvated clusters for Mg2+-ion and Li+-ion were calculated based on the paths involving sequential solvent detachment and anion dissociation. The energy barrier (E desol:) of stepwise desolvation was calculated by the following equation:

E desol: = E solvent=ion + E res: − E tot: (3)

where E solvent=ion, E res:, and E tot: represent the energies of stripped species (THF solvent, Cl⁻, or [TPFPB-Cl]⁻), residual stable configuration after stripping, and initial stable configuration before desolvation step, respectively. Supplementary Data 7–10 provide the initial and final configurations of the solvated clusters for the hexa-coordinated Mg2+(THF)5Cl⁻ and tetra-coordinated Li+(THF)3Cl− with and without TPFPB mediation during structure optimization.

The structural relaxation of FeOF and Li0.5FeOF was performed by DFT calculation using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP, version 5.3.3) with Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof parametrization of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA). The projector-augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials (version 5.2) were implemented in VASP to describe the electron-ion interaction. The PAW pseudopotentials and valence configurations for each atom used in DFT calculations are: Mg_pv(2p63s2) for magnesium, Li_sv(1s22s1) for lithium, Fe_pv(3p63d74s1) for iron, O(2s22p4) for oxygen, and F(2s22p5) for fluorine. Considering the strong correlation character of Fe 3d electrons, a Hubbard-type correction (GGA+U) with a Ueff value of 5.0 eV was applied66. A gamma-centered k-points mesh of 5×5×5 was used to sample the Brillouin zone for both FeOF and Li0.5FeOF. The activation barrier and migration pathway for charge-carrier (Mg2+ or Li+) hopping were estimated by the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method67. The potential migration pathways were constructed using the linear interpolation between initial and final states, and the structures were then relaxed with a maximum residual force threshold of 0.05 eV Å−1 for each atom. The cutoff energy was set to 450 eV, and the energy convergence criteria for structure relaxation were less than 10−6 eV. The force convergence criterion was set as 0.02 eV Å−1 for the structural relaxation of initial FeOF and Li0.5FeOF. The energy convergence criterion was less than 10−6 eV for both structure relaxations and CI-NEB calculations. The cutoff energy was set to 450 eV in all the calculations. The crystal structures of FeOF and Li0.5FeOF are obtained from Material Project68 and re-constructed according to the previous study48 using VESTA software (version 3.4.0)69. The crystal structures, clusters and differential charge density maps are visualized using VESTA software69. The schematic illustrations of the regulating effect of TPFPB on electrolyte and the reaction mechanism of FeOF co-driven by Li/Mg-ions, as well as the format backgrounds of electrochemical performance diagrams, are generated using PowerPoint software. Supplementary Data 11, 12 provide the optimized structures of FeOF and Li0.5FeOF with Mg-ion intercalation.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
We thank the authors for the interesting application of a FeOxFy cathode to a Mg/Li hybrid battery. We've noticed a number of gaps in the manuscript that should be addressed.
(1) Confirm the stoichiometry of the FeOxFy compound by ion chromatography AND confirm the density of the cathode material relative to the proposed crystal structure. The stoichiometry of FeOxF2-x (0 ≤ x ≤ 1) with x=0.7 implies an odd assortment of FexOy phases in addition to FeF3 that are potentially inactive.
(2) Report the CE after 1, 10, and 50 cycles of asymmetric Mg/current collector cell cycling at 1 mAh/cm.sq with the control and TPFPB-containing electrolyte.
(3) Report the mass loading (mg/cm.sq) of the cathode, its thickness, the n/p ratio, and electrolyte loading.
(4) Report the average CE and capacity loss (%) for the first 10 cycles of the full cell tests with the control and TPFPB-containing electrolyte tests at 2.5, 2.7 and 3.0 V in the revised manuscript. This data will be important for readers wanting to optimize initial capacity loss and electrolyte consumption.
(5) Please measure the conductivity of the control and TPFPB-containing electrolyte
(6) Report LSV measurements with a reference electrode. Otherwise overpotentials on the counter electrode can inflate the oxidative stability of the electrolyte.
Additional comments on the computational efforts:
(1) The Gaussian09 software should be cited, additionally the revision number should be given (e.g., D.01).
(2) A more standard practice for denoting calculations with geometry optimization at one level of theory and single point calculations at another is B3LYP/6-311+G(d,p)//M06-2X/def2-TZVP; the methods and basis sets should be cited as well. Use the EMSL Basis Set Exchange to obtain the necessary references for the various basis sets.
(3) Please provide version information for the Multiwfn and VMD codes used to process and visualize the ESPs.
(4) The authors are missing a number of essential details to produce the calculations, see below...
(a)Please provide the version of the code and pseudopotentials used; they may be different (e.g., current version of the code is 6.5.1 but you can pair it with pseudopotentials from version 5.2, 5.4, or 6.4 (see https://www.vasp.at/wiki/index.php/Available_pseudopotentials)
(b) For the psuedopotentials, please provide which specific potential names were per element, Mg vs Mg_pv, for example.
(c) For the climbing image NEB method, if you are using the VTST patch, please cite the corresponding Henkelman paper. KPOINTS settings should be reported as well.
(d) If structures were downloaded or accessed via a database (e.g., Materials Project, etc.), please provide a reference to the specific structure pulled.
(e) Any of the following settings should be reported if necessary, if dispersion corrections were used, if Hubbard corrections were used (include which element(s) and the +U energy), please distinguish between initial bulk relaxations of FeOF and Li0.5FeOF and the subsequent NEB calculations. Some settings are unlikely to be preserved between these methods.
(5) For the visuals of the crystal structure and cluster calculations, please cite the visualization software used to produce the images.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In the manuscript, the authors proposed a novel Mg-fluoride battery prototype. The introduction of anion receptors into electrolyte enhances the oxidative stability and modulates the solvation structure, enabling Mg-fluoride batteries with satisfactory electrochemical performance. The conversion reaction mechanism involving dual-cation co-participation in fluorides is elucidated in depth using a combination of DFT calculations and solid characterizations. This work achieves an advance in expanding the cathode options for Mg-based batteries to high-energy fluoride cathodes. The beneficial role of anion receptors in mitigating the interfacial issues of chloride-containing electrolytes is also an interesting finding. Overall, the publication in Nature Communications is recommended after some minor issues are addressed.
(1) The magnesium chloride cations are thermodynamically stable due to the high scission energy. It is interesting to find that the Cl-related interfacial reaction activity is suppressed while enabling Mg participation in cathode reactions. Please give a detailed explanation about this phenomenon.
(2) After introducing the TPFPB additive, the APC electrolyte has demonstrated an extended electrochemical window and enhanced corrosion resistance. Is there a supportive explanation or other proof for this point?
(3) For the electrochemical performance in Figure 3, why does the Mg full cell exhibit the better cycling stability and higher CE at a low temperature of –20 °C compared to at room temperature?
(4) The activation barriers for cation diffusion in rutile-structured FeOF vary significantly along different paths. Anion coordination environment should play a critical role, meriting further explanation to clarify its impact.
(5) According to the DRT results, the charge-transfer-related peaks within a timescale range of 10-2–1 s show the distinct evolution behaviors during the charge and discharge processes. This appears to suggest distinct reaction mechanisms. Please discuss the possible underlying reasons.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
Chen et al. reported the oxyfluoride FeO0.7F1.3 as a cathode material for magnesium metal batteries, and employed a TPFPB-mediated electrolyte to mitigate interfacial side reactions, thereby achieving stable high-voltage operation. The TPFPB-mediated solvation environment reduces the desolvation energy barrier, further contributing to high-capacity and low-temperature-tolerant Mg-FeO0.7F1.3 cells. The development of fluoride-based magnesium batteries is novel and may be of great value. The electrochemical performance is impressive, and the underlying understanding of the reaction mechanism is provided. I consider that a minor revision is necessary before the acceptance of this manuscript. My specific comments are listed below.
1. The authors performed detailed DFT calculations to analyze the regulation effect of TPFPB on cation solvation structures. However, the related regulation mechanism requires further clarification. Additionally, experimental evidence supporting the change in solvation environment should be provided.
2. Figure 1e shows a significant improvement in electrolyte oxidation stability upon TPFPB addition. The authors ascribe this to altered chemical components in the electrolyte. They are suggested to explain clearly how TPFPB affect the electrolyte oxidation stability by changing the chemical components.
3. The intercalation-type cells exhibit the divergence in Coulombic efficiency during the later stages of long-term cycling. What might be the potential causes of this behavior?
4. Regarding the dual-cation co-driven reaction mechanism, whether Mg2+ ions or MgCl+ species are involved in the cathode reactions?
5. Why is the ion migration kinetics enhanced in the FeOF structure following partial lithiation reaction?
6. Does the acceptor additive participate in the formation of the CEI layer observed in the TEM images?

To investigate the density of as-prepared FeO F , the compaction density under different pressures has been obtained using a four-probe method for powder testing (as seen in the following Figure). Response to "The stoichiometry of FeO F (0 ≤ x ≤ 1) with x=0.7 implies an odd assortment of Fe O phases in addition to FeF that are potentially inactive":
We propose the reaction mechanism of iron oxyfluoride driven by dual-cationic charge carriers in Fig. 5I (as seen below), which also reveals the role of oxygen component in the reversible cycle of oxyfluoride cathode. The discharge process enables the solid-solution-like electrochemical lithiation, followed by the Li+/Mg2+ co-driven conversion reactions that result in the retained RS-phase Li FeO and extruded Fe metal, LiF and MgF (in the confined voltage). The cubic lattice coherence and similar lattice constants of these discharge products tend to promote the local electronic and ionic transport at multiphase interfaces. It has a positive effect on the reinjection of Fe/F components into Li FeO upon the delithiation/demagnesiation (charge) process, thus being advantageous to reconstitute the parent structure and maintain the particle integrity. Therefore, although the Fe O moiety in iron oxyfluorides is not fully activated (i.e., it does not participate in the conversion reaction), the retained Li FeO intermediate could serve as a favorable substrate structure to promote the reconstitution of parent oxyfluoride structure. Compared with the FeF cathode, which undergoes the deep phase transformation during conversion reaction, the FeO F cathodes typically deliver the higher kinetic capacity at the expense of thermodynamic capacity based on the partial conversion reaction mode.
On the other hand, the oxygen/fluorine substitution in rutile-type FeF enables the solid solution form of FeII FeIII O F (0 ≤ x ≤ 1), indicating that oxygen (1~x) x x 2~x doping will increase the valence state of Fe and boost the theoretical capacity for oxyfluorides (from 571 mAh g-1 for FeF to 884 mAh g-1 for FeOF). The increased Fe3+ content in FeO F could enhance the intercalation reaction in high voltage region. Overall, the introduction of oxygen into oxyfluoride cathodes facilitates their sustainable cycling with high capacity and high energy release.
We have added the corresponding discussion in Page 23.

(2) Report the CE after 1, 10, and 50 cycles of asymmetric Mg/current collector cell cycling at 1 mAh/cm.sq with the control and TPFPB-containing electrolyte.
Response: Thanks for the valuable suggestion! To evaluate the reversibility of Mg plating/stripping in the baseline APC-type electrolyte and TPFPB-containing electrolyte, we have galvanostatically measured the coulombic efficiency (CE) of Mg||Cu asymmetric cells at a current density of 0.5 mA cm-2 and an areal capacity of 1.0 mAh cm-2 (as seen below as newly added Supplementary Fig. 5). As shown in Supplementary Fig. 5A, the initial CE of Mg||Cu asymmetric cell in LiCl-APC electrolyte is 91.89% and the CE gradually increases in subsequent cycles, reaching 98.68% and 99.37% after 10 and 50 cycles, respectively. However, an abnormal increase in overpotential, accompanied by a jitter in charge curve, is observed before the Mg stripping step is completed (Supplementary Fig. 5B). This unstable Mg stripping behavior is likely due to the anodic corrosion of Cu collector caused by the baseline APC-type electrolyte. For the asymmetric cell using LiCl-APC-TPFPB electrolyte, the TPFPB with electron-withdrawing character tends to undergo reduction decomposition and promote SEI formation during the first Mg plating step, resulting in a relatively low initial CE of 74.28%. Nevertheless, the CEs quickly recover to the values comparable to those of LiCl-APC case with the progress of cycling, reaching 95.50% and 99.26% after 10 and 50 cycles, respectively. Different from the control case, the Mg||Cu cell with TPFPB-containing electrolyte can maintain the flat voltage profiles during long-term Mg plating/stripping cycles (Supplementary Fig. 5C), which should benefit from the key role of anion receptor in inhibiting Cl-associated corrosion. These results indicate the highly reversible and stable Mg plating/stripping behavior enabled by the TPFPB-mediated electrolyte.

In this work, we first proposed a rechargeable magnesium-fluoride battery prototype that promises a further improvement in the energy density of MMBs. We focus on developing a reversible and sustainable electrochemical system with FeO F cathode and Mg anode enabled by electrolyte design, and systematically demonstrating the dual-cation co-driven reaction mechanisms. (4) Report the average CE and capacity loss (%) for the first 10 cycles of the full cell tests with the control and TPFPB-containing electrolyte tests at 2.5, 2.7 and 3.0 V in the revised manuscript. Response: Thanks for the valuable suggestion! We have presented the average CE and capacity loss for the first 10 cycles of Mg-FeO F cells using LiCl-APC and LiCl-APC-TPFPB electrolytes in newly added Supplementary Figs. 17 and 18 (as seen below). For the conversion-type cells (Supplementary Fig. 17), a low average CE value of 77% is yielded in the LiCl-APC system, which should result from the severe interfacial side reactions due to the poor oxidation stability of electrolyte. Moreover, the converted metallic iron in cycled fluoride cathode is susceptible to the anodic corrosion from Cl-based electrolyte and has a potential catalytic effect on interfacial side reaction. By comparison, using the LiCl-APC-TPFPB electrolyte with enhanced anti-oxidation ability, the Mg-FeO F cells perform the higher average CE values (in a range of 87%–94%) for the first 10 cycles, even at the higher charge cut-off voltages. Benefiting from its high-voltage tolerance, the LiCl-APC-TPFPB electrolyte enables the 3.0 V class cell to achieve good cycling stability with the lowering of capacity loss to 28%, compared with 44% of capacity loss for the 2.5 V class cell using LiCl-APC electrolyte. For the intercalation-type cells, the decreased phase transformation degree and reduced volume variation can mitigate the surface activity-related side reactions of fluoride cathodes. Consequently, the Mg-FeO F cells with two APC-type electrolytes both deliver the higher levels of CE, with the TPFPB-containing systems still exhibiting the relatively higher average CE values (in a range of 91%-96%) for the first 10 cycles (Supplementary Fig. 18). A reduction in capacity loss of Mg-FeO F cells from 50% to 32% can be achieved when TPFPB is added to the APC-type electrolyte. Overall, from the performance perspective, the initial capacity loss and coulombic efficiency need to be further improved in future studies on the emerging Mg-fluoride batteries. Our study presents a promising research direction to develop electrolyte materials with a wide electrochemical window, enabling the good compatibilities with both high-potential fluoride cathodes and passivation-sensitive Mg anodes.

Response: Based on the reviewer’s suggestion, we have measured the ionic conductivities of baseline APC-type electrolyte and TPFPB-containing electrolyte by a DDSJ-308A conductivity meter (Leici) at room temperature (as seen below as newly added Supplementary Fig. 4). The addition of TPFPB additive, which has a relatively large molecular structure, would more or less increase the viscosity of electrolyte and decrease its bulk ion mobility. On the other hand, as an anion receptor, TPFPB can enhance the dissociation of chloride salts by coordinating with Cl ligands, thereby promoting the cation migration in bulk electrolyte and across interfaces/interphases. As a result, two-type electrolytes exhibit the comparable ionic conductivities of 2.96×10-3 and 2.92×10-3 S cm-1 for LiCl-APC and LiCl-APC-TPFPB, respectively.

(6) Report LSV measurements with a reference electrode. Otherwise overpotentials on the counter electrode can inflate the oxidative stability of the electrolyte.
Response: Thanks for the careful review of our manuscript. Based on the reviewer’s suggestion, we have re-evaluated the intrinsic oxidative stability of two APC-type electrolytes in a three-electrode configuration, using Mg foils as reference and counter electrodes (as seen below as newly added Fig. 1E). In the baseline LiCl-APC electrolyte systems with SS and Mo working electrodes, the oxidation onset potentials of ~2.14 and ~2.53 V vs. Mg/Mg2+ are observed, respectively. To reviewer #2 and reviewer #3：
In the manuscript, the authors proposed a novel Mg-fluoride battery prototype. The introduction of anion receptors into electrolyte enhances the oxidative stability and modulates the solvation structure, enabling Mg-fluoride batteries with satisfactory electrochemical performance. The conversion reaction mechanism involving dual-cation co-participation in fluorides is elucidated in depth using a combination of DFT calculations and solid characterizations. This work achieves an advance in expanding the cathode options for Mg-based batteries to high-energy fluoride cathodes. The beneficial role of anion receptors in mitigating the interfacial issues of chloride-containing electrolytes is also an interesting finding. Overall, the publication in Nature Communications is recommended after some minor issues are addressed.
Response: Thanks for the positive and insightful comments from the reviewers. We have improved our work based on the following detailed comments proposed by the reviewers.
(1) The magnesium chloride cations are thermodynamically stable due to the high scission energy. It is interesting to find that the Cl-related interfacial reaction activity is suppressed while enabling Mg participation in cathode reactions. Please give a detailed explanation about this phenomenon.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s comment. According to the quantum chemical calculations (Fig. 1A), TPFPB receptor shows the strong electrostatic attraction with magnesium chloride complexes with the binding energies of −1.06, −1.18, and −1.33 eV for MgCl+, MgCl , and Mg Cl +, respectively. Note that the absorbed Mg Cl + 2 2 3 2 3 cluster on TPFPB undergoes structural deformation (Supplementary Fig. 1), where one of the chlorine atoms breaks the original Mg-Cl-Mg bridge and approaches the boron center of anion receptor. It seems that the introduction of TPFPB is unfavorable for the stable existence of Mg Cl + species in APC solution. Driven by the 2 3 TPFPB-induced interaction, the Raman peak related to [Mg Cl ·6THF]+ becomes 2 3 somewhat blurred and shows an evident blue shift from 245 cm-1 to 252 cm-1 (Fig. 1D). This confirms the structural instability of Mg Cl + species when interacting with 2 3 TPFPB. As a major culprit for corrosion, the decreased concentration of [Mg Cl ·6THF]+ is expected to alleviate the corrosivity of 2 3 TPFPB-mediated electrolyte. On the other hand, according to the DFT calculations on ion desolvation processes (Fig. 2C), the energy barrier for rate-determining Mg2+-Cl⁻ scission is substantially lowered from 3.07 eV to 2.09 eV, and it is facilitated by the formation of thermodynamically stable [TPFPB-Cl]⁻ complex. Overall, the strong electrostatic attraction between TPFPB and chlorine ligand can promote the dechlorination process of Mg2+ cation and alleviate the Cl-related side reactions at cathode-electrolyte interface.
Please see the corresponding discussion in Page 6, 8, and Page 11-12.
(2) After introducing the TPFPB additive, the APC electrolyte has demonstrated an extended electrochemical window and enhanced corrosion resistance. Is there a supportive explanation or other proof for this point?
Response: Based on the reviewer’s suggestions, we have disassembled the Mg//SS cells that underwent the anodic scan of LSV measurements and observed the corrosive state on the surface of SS current collectors. The corresponding optical images of SS current collectors are presented in Supplementary Fig. 3. After the anodic scanning to 3.3 V in the baseline APC-type solution, severe corrosion occurs on the SS surface, which is fully covered by thick and white by-products. For the TPFPB-containing system, even at a higher termination potential of 4.0 V, the anodic current is decreased and only some thin coverages are observed in the local region, indicating that the corrosion phenomenon is significantly mitigated.
Please see the corresponding discussion in Page 8-9.
Supplementary Figure 3. LSV curves of Li-SS asymmetric cells with APC-type electrolytes at a scan rate of 0.1 mV s-1 and the optical images of collected SS after LSV measurements.
(3) For the electrochemical performance in Figure 3, why does the Mg full cell exhibit the better cycling stability and higher CE at a low temperature of –20 °C compared to at room temperature?
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s comment. Lowering temperature typically reduces the Mg-cation participation in cathode reaction due to the diffusion-limited reactivity, which is favorable for the reversible electrochemistry of dominated lithiation-driven phase transformation in fluoride. Meanwhile, the interfacial side reactions such as Cl-corrosion and Fe-dissolution are expected to be further mitigated in the low-temperature environment. These effects should be responsible for the improved cycling stability with a lower capacity decay rate of 0.18% per cycle for Mg-FeO F cell when the temperature is switched from room temperature to – 0.7 1.3 20 °C. The alleviated anodic corrosion also contributes to the high average CE value of 98%.
Please see the corresponding discussion in Page 17.
(4) The activation barriers for cation diffusion in rutile-structured FeOF vary significantly along different paths. Anion coordination environment should play a critical role, meriting further explanation to clarify its impact.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s valuable comment. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 27, there are three anion channels (i.e. mixed O/F, F, and O channels) along [001] direction, which provide the potential pathways (denoted as path 1, 2, and 3, respectively) for cation migration in rutile-type FeOF structure. Along the three paths, the intercalated cations can pass through the metastable octahedral sites when hopping between adjacent stable octahedral sites (Fig. 5B), which requires activation energy to overcome the corresponding energy barrier. The calculated energy barriers of path 1, 2, and 3 for Li-ion migration are 1.39, 0.18, and 4.40 eV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 27F). The highest energy barrier of path 3 should be attributed to the strong electrostatic interaction between intercalated cation and bivalent lattice O2- with concentrated charge nature. The electrostatic force also drives the Fe atoms to move off-center towards the O atoms, thereby increasing the Fe3+-Li+ repulsion in O channel due to shortened distance (Supplementary Fig. 27E). As a result, the octahedral sites for Li occupation are in off-center positions after lattice relaxation (Supplementary Fig. 27D). It can be deduced that the lithiation sites within the mixed and F channels (denoted as H1 and H2 respectively) are more energetically favorable or stable than t hose within the O channels (Fig. 5A).

This phenomenon suggests the asymmetric conversion paths for oxyfluoride cathode during discharge and charge, as further verified by the observed asymmetric redox peaks in CV profiles (Supplementary Fig. 11). In the late charge, the τ peak splits into a blurred doublet that likely corresponds to the 4 partitioned reconstitution pathways of F-rich rutile and O-rich RS phases. To reviewer #4 and reviewer #5：
Chen et al. reported the oxyfluoride FeO F as a cathode material for magnesium 0.7 1.3 metal batteries, and employed a TPFPB-mediated electrolyte to mitigate interfacial side reactions, thereby achieving stable high-voltage operation. The TPFPB-mediated solvation environment reduces the desolvation energy barrier, further contributing to high-capacity and low-temperature-tolerant Mg-FeO F cells. The development of 0.7 1.3 fluoride-based magnesium batteries is novel and may be of great value. The electrochemical performance is impressive, and the underlying understanding of the reaction mechanism is provided. I consider that a minor revision is necessary before the acceptance of this manuscript. My specific comments are listed below.
Response: Thanks for the positive and insightful comments from the reviewers. We have improved our work based on the following detailed comments proposed by the reviewers.
1. The authors performed detailed DFT calculations to analyze the regulation effect of TPFPB on cation solvation structures. However, the related regulation mechanism requires further clarification. Additionally, experimental evidence supporting the change in solvation environment should be provided.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s comment. In the APC-type solutions where Mg²⁺ and Li⁺ ions are typically coordinated by a combination of Cl- and THF ligands, we employed quantum chemistry simulations to optimize the solvated configurations of both Mg-ion (i.e. Mg2+(THF)ₙCl⁻) and Li-ion (i.e. Li+(THF)ₙCl⁻), systematically comparing the cases with and without TPFPB mediation (Supplementary Figs. 6-9). Although the receptor additive is not directly involved in the inner solvation sheath of cationic species, it can loosen the solvation structures via the TPFPB-induced dipole-ion (B···Cl-) interaction with chloride ions and the dipole-dipole interaction (F···H-C) with THF molecules (Fig. 2A). As shown in Fig. 2B, the introduction of TPFPB extends the Mg···Cl distance between Mg2+ and Cl- as well as the average Mg···O distance between Mg2+ and THF for Mg solvation complexes. Similar trends are seen for the Li solvation complexes in terms of Li···Cl and Li···O coordination distances (Fig. 2C).

To further understand the weak solvation effect, 7Li NMR measurements were performed on the LiCl-APC and LiCl-APC-TPFPB electrolytes (Fig. 2D). A downfield shift in the 7Li signal of solvated lithium salt is observed upon the addition of TPFPB to the baseline APC-type electrolyte, correspondingly moving from δ = 0.53 to 0.69 ppm. This result confirms the deshielding effect of receptor additive on the cations in electrolyte, which weakens the coordination of cations with electron-donating Cl⁻ ions and ethereal O groups of THF solvent.

Fig. 2D 7Li NMR spectra of LiCl-APC-TPFPB (top) and LiCl-APC (bottom) electrolytes.
2. Figure 1e shows a significant improvement in electrolyte oxidation stability upon TPFPB addition. The authors ascribe this to altered chemical components in the electrolyte. They are suggested to explain clearly how TPFPB affect the electrolyte oxidation stability by changing the chemical components.

Driven by the TPFPB-induced interaction, the Raman peak related to [Mg Cl ·6THF]+ becomes somewhat blurred and shows an 2 3 evident blue shift from 245 cm-1 to 252 cm-1. Meanwhile, the Raman signal related to MgCl ·4THF at 212 cm-1 is intensified. It is deduced that TPFPB appears to inhibit 2 the reaction equilibrium in which MgCl+ and MgCl together form the Mg Cl + 2 2 3 species. The reduction in Mg Cl + is consistent with the result of its structural 2 3 instability when interacting with TPFPB, as indicated by the DFT calculation shown in Supplementary Fig. 1. As a major culprit for corrosion, the decreased concentration of [Mg Cl ·6THF]+ is expected to alleviate the corrosivity of 2 3 TPFPB-mediated electrolyte. It can be observed that the peak at 993 cm-1 attributed to the metal-phenyl ring vibration of Ph Al- decreases in intensity, while the peak at 4 345 cm-1 attributed to AlCl - increases in intensity. The decreased concentration of 4 the most oxidation-vulnerable Ph Al- in exchange for the increased concentration 4 of the most oxidation-resistant AlCl - can contribute to the enhancement of 4 high-voltage tolerance for the TPFPB-containing APC system.

3. The intercalation-type cells exhibit the divergence in Coulombic efficiency during the later stages of long-term cycling. What might be the potential causes of this behavior?
Response: As shown in Supplementary Fig. 13, the initial discharge profile displays the sole solid solution reaction stage without involving the conversion reaction, offering a dominant plateau at ~1.75 V with a capacity beyond 200 mAh g-1. As the cycling proceeds, the cell with LiCl-APC electrolyte suffers from the evident plateau degradation and capacity decrease. Note that the second-stage discharge plateau appears at below ~1.5 V after 200 cycles (Supplementary Fig. 13A), indicating the occurrence of conversion reaction in fluoride cathode. The accumulation of converted metallic Fe is prone to induce anodic corrosion and parasitic side reactions, which should be responsible for the sharp CE decline in subsequent cycling (Fig. 3F). In comparison, the modified cell with TPFPB addition can well maintain the sloped intercalation plateau within 300 cycles without involving conversion reaction (Supplementary Fig. 13B).

4. Regarding the dual-cation co-driven reaction mechanism, whether Mg2+ ions or MgCl+ species are involved in the cathode reactions?
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s comment. From the XPS concentration-depth profiles of the discharged FeO F cathode (Supplementary Fig. 26), the atomic 0.7 1.3 fractions of Cl and Al elements show a descending trend with etching, which is different from those of the active elements such as Fe, F, Li, and Mg. Correspondingly, the Mg-F and Mg-Cl components show the opposite concentration evolutions from surface to subsurface, according to the increased peak area for Mg-F and decreased peak area for Mg-Cl in Mg 1s spectra (Supplementary Fig. 25D). It can be deduced that the detected Cl-based species are mainly residual chloride salts covering the cathode surface and are not deeply involved in fluoride reactions. Consequently, due to the dechlorination effect of TPFPB, the magnesiation reactions of fluoride cathode should be mainly dominated by Mg2+ ions rather than MgCl+ species.

5. Why is the ion migration kinetics enhanced in the FeOF structure following partial lithiation reaction?
Response: Based on the reviewer’s suggestion, we first analyzed the DFT-relaxed structures of FeOF and Li FeOF. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 29, it causes the 0.5 obvious lattice expansion along b-axis with the elongation of Fe-F and Fe-O bonds from FeOF to Li FeOF. Notably, the volume of octahedral site for further cation 0.5 occupation along the empty mixed O/F channel correspondingly increases by 29%. On the other hand, the Li-cation pre-intercalation also has an impact on the electron redistribution upon subsequent Mg insertion in Li FeOF. The differential 0.5 charge density of Mg-ion intercalated in FeOF (Fig. 5C) shows a pronounced charge transfer from divalent Mg-ion to FeOF host, leading to the formation of charge depletion zone around Mg and charge accumulation region around adjacent O and F atoms. This explains why the migration kinetics of Mg-ions in FeOF structure is sluggish (Fig. 5D). As for Li FeOF, the charge accumulation on O/F ligands 0.5 near Mg ion is markedly reduced (Fig. 5G), implying the weakened interaction between intercalated Mg-ion and Li FeOF host. Overall, the expanded channel 0.5 spacing and weakened electrostatic interaction are expected to enhance the cation mobility along mixed O/F path (Fig. 5F), lowering the migration energy barriers to 0.50 eV for Li-ions and to 2.32 eV for Mg-ions (Fig. 5H).

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Rechargeable magnesium batteries have emerged as a competitive next-generation energy storage technology owing to their abundant resources and inherent safety. The development of Mg batteries, especially regarding specific energy, has been compromised by the lack of high-performance positive electrodes. Here, we design an anion-receptor-mediated all-phenyl-complex electrolyte that enables the electrochemical cooperation between fluoride and magnesium, and develop a Mg||FeO0.7F1.3 battery prototype. The anion receptor of tris(pentafluorophenyl)borane alters the chemical compositions of electrolyte and regulates its solvation structures via dipole-ion and dipole-dipole interactions with chloride-based ionic species and solvent molecules. The tailored electrolyte mitigates the chloride-originated anodic instability and upgrades the desolvation kinetics of cationic carriers. The dual-cation co-driven conversion-type Mg||FeO0.7F1.3 batteries exhibit the high reversible capacities in a wide temperature range, delivering 354 mAh g⁻¹ at 25 °C and 177 mAh g⁻¹ at –20 °C. Moreover, the high reversibility over 500 cycles with a low capacity decay rate of 0.054% per cycle can be realized when confined to intercalation chemistry. This work provides an anion receptor-based electrolyte design strategy that expands positive material horizons for magnesium batteries to high-energy fluorides.

---

## Introduction

Although lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have dominated the energy storage market, including portable electronic devices and electric vehicles, the inherent problems of high cost (resource shortage) and safety concern (Li dendrite growth) limit their applications in large-scale energy storage systems1. As an alternative, magnesium metal batteries (MMBs) have received increasing attention owing to the abundant Mg element (the 8th most abundant in the earth’s crust) and the utilization of Mg metal negative electrode, which can offer the high volumetric capacity of 3833 mAh cm−3 (~1.8 times that of Li metal) and relatively low redox potential of −2.37 V (versus standard hydrogen electrode)2. In particular, due to the less reactive nature compared with Li metal, Mg metal shows a low tendency to the occurrence of dendrite propagation and internal short circuit of MMBs during electrochemical stripping/plating cycling2. Therefore, MMBs have great potential to develop into the next-generation energy storage technology (beyond LIBs) that can meet the requirements of safety, sustainability and high performance. However, the bivalent Mg2+ with high charge density induces the great electrostatic interaction with host lattices and strong ligand binding in solvation, which results in sluggish mass transport kinetics in bulk electrode and electrolyte as well as at their solid-liquid interfaces3,4. While substantial progress has been made in the electrode interface engineering that facilitates the reversible Mg stripping/plating5–7, the further advancement of MMBs is still hindered by lacking high-energy and high-capacity positive electrodes.

Uptonow, the widely used positive electrode materials in MMBs are mainly limited to chalcogenides and oxides. Transition-metal chalcogenides with “soft” anion sublattices can weaken the Mg2+-host interaction due to the enhanced structure polarizability, thereby contributing to the bivalent cation mobility in solid-state frameworks8,9. But even so, the reversible Mg-intercalated capacities are typically less than 110 mAh g−1 for Chevrel Mo6S8 and 200 mAh g−1 for thiospinel Ti2S4 10–12, even under the favorable operating conditions (e.g., a low current rate of 0.1 C and an elevated temperature of 60 oC). Although the conversion-type sulfides (e.g., FeS2 and CuS2) can deliver the higher specific capacities, the cycling stability is severely compromised by poor reaction kinetics and potential shuttle effect of polysulfide intermediates13,14. More unfortunately, chalcogenide compounds typically only offer a low discharge potential of ~1.0 V vs. Mg2+/Mg, which inherently restricts the specific energy improvement for MMBs. Substituting chalcogenide with oxide clusters (e.g., V2O5 and MnO2) can theoretically raise the output voltage15,16. However, Mg2+-ions suffer from a high diffusion barrier in oxide lattices due to their strong affinity to O2−, which is also prone to induce the extrusion of Mg oxide rather than following a complete intercalation route during electrochemical reaction16. To optimize the Mg2+-diffusion environment, structure pillaring is an effective strategy, especially for two-dimensional layered materials with high structure tunability. The bilayer-structured V2O5·H2O materials have been developed for hosting multivalent ions, benefiting from the dual effects of interlayer expansion and electrostatic shielding by lattice water17–19. For instance, the hydrated V2O5 with Mg2+ ion pre-intercalation enables a reversible and stable Mg2+-storage capacity of ~164 mAh g−1 under a specific current of 0.1 A g−117. Despite the enhanced Mg-insertion reactivity, it is at the expense of practical output voltage (in the range of −1.0–1.0 V) since using active carbon as the negative material instead of Mg metal. The compromised choice of negative electrode should be attributed to the electrolyte incompatibility and inevitable release of crystal water into electrolyte, which induce the undesired interfacial side reactions and surface passivation of Mg metal17,18. In addition to H2O, some organic molecules such as poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene (PEDOT) and cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) also can serve as intercalation agents to upgrade the Mg2+ diffusion kinetic14,20. Nevertheless, introducing the electrochemically inactive and large-size pillars would markedly decrease the specific energy in both gravimetric and volumetric levels (e.g., the interlayer spacing of V2O5 is more than doubled by PEDOT pillaring). Overall, it is necessary and urgent to explore the energy-dense positive electrode materials for advanced MMBs.

Compared with oxides and chalcogenide counterparts, metal fluorides with the high electronegativity F-ligand can yield the higher thermodynamic equilibrium potentials21. Among them, the resource-abundant and cost-efficient iron trifluoride (FeF3) has been widely investigated recently and identified as promising energy-dense positive electrode (with a considerable value of 1947 Wh kg−1) in LIBs, based on a thermodynamic potential of ~2.73 V (vs. Li+/Li) and a high theoretical capacity of 712 mAh g−1 via three-electron transfer reaction22. Therefore, exploring the electrochemical cooperation between iron fluoride positive electrode and Mg metal negative electrode will promote the development of high-energy Mg-based battery prototypes. However, conversion-type magnesium-fluoride batteries may be challenging in efficient operation when relying exclusively on Mg²⁺ ion shuttling. This is primarily due to the slow kinetics associated with divalent carriers, which involve the solid diffusion through dense and rigid fluoride structure, as well as the breaking and reformation of strong metal-fluorine bonds21. Inspired by Mg-based hybrid batteries, magnesium-fluoride conversion systems are expected to be activated by using dual-salt electrolytes, which enable the combination of kinetically favorable monovalent (e.g., Li+) chemistry at positive electrode and thermodynamically dominant Mg stripping/plating at negative electrode23. In this regard, fluoride choice for Mg-based hybrid batteries can more or less follow the structure design method that has been established in lithium batteries. Given the above-mentioned negative impacts of lattice water on electrolyte stability and compatibility with Mg metal, the typical open-framework strategy via H2O stuffing seems unavailable on conversion-type fluorides involving phase-separation reactions in MMBs. Mixed anion chemistry with O-substitution for fluorides could improve the intrinsic electronic conductivity and ionic mobility due to the weakened bond ionicity24. Moreover, it is also expected to regulate the phase evolution pathway and mitigate the phase separation within a confined voltage range25. Consequently, the kinetic capacity can be enhanced despite a certain loss in thermodynamic capacity.

Herein, we developed a rechargeable magnesium-fluoride battery prototype that promises a further improvement in the specific energy of MMBs. The electrochemical system comprises the iron oxyfluoride (FeO0.7F1.3) positive electrode and the electrolyte based on an all-phenyl-complex (APC) solution mediated by an anion receptor of tris(pentafluorophenyl)borane (TPFPB). As a strong Lewis acid, the TPFPB molecule exhibits the strong interactions with Cl-based ionic species and alters their charge distribution through electron-withdrawing effects. Meanwhile, it affects the equilibrium species of Lewis acid-base reactions in APC-type solution with tetrahydrofuran (THF) solvent, resulting in the decreased concentration of magnesium dimer cation [Mg2Cl3·6THF]+ (a major culprit for corrosion). Consequently, the modified electrolyte is able to inhibit the anodic corrosion on current collector and enhance the high voltage tolerance (up to 3.71 V vs. Mg2+/Mg using Mo foil). Moreover, the TPFPB-induced dipole-dipole/ion interactions loosen the solvation structures of APC-type electrolyte, thereby reducing the desolvation barriers for both Mg2+ and Li+ cations. Benefitting from the enhanced oxidative stability and interfacial reaction kinetics of electrolyte, the conversion-type Mg||FeO0.7F1.3 batteries deliver the reversible capacities as high as 354 mAh g−1 at room temperature (25 °C) as well as 177 mAh g⁻¹ at low temperature (−20 °C). When confining the fluoride activation to intercalation reaction stage, the cells enable a high average discharge voltage of 1.77 V and good cycling stability, sustaining over 500 cycles with a low capacity decay rate of 0.054% per cycle. This work broadens the positive electrode material option for MMBs and provides a promising avenue to develop an energy-dense, high-safety, and low-cost energy storage technology. The proposed anion receptor chemistry offers an effective solution to the interfacial issue of chloride-based electrolytes in high-voltage applications.
