## Methods

Synthesis of fluoride
The FeO0.7F1.3 was prepared by a facile thermal treatment of hydrate iron fluoride, which was obtained based on a dissolution-precipitation method in an ionic liquid medium25. Firstly, a certain amount of Ketjen Black (KB, Shenzhen Kejing Zhida Technology Co., Ltd., 25 wt% in the final weight of fluoride composite) was added into 10 mL of ionic liquid 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate (BmimBF4, Aladdin, 98%), followed by vigorous stirring at 50 °C for several hours to form a uniform black solution. Then, it was transferred into the ice-water bath and cooled down to 0 °C, and 1.0 g of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (Aladdin, 98%) was gradually added into the KB-suspended solution under stirring state. The reaction solution was kept stirred for 12 h at the ice-water bath to allow sufficient fluorination. The precipitate product (FeF3·3H2O/KB) was washed with acetone (Adamas, 99.9%) and centrifuged several times, followed by drying under vacuum at 80 °C for 12 h. Finally, the hydrate iron fluoride composite was heated at 300 °C for 5 h with a ramping rate of 5 °C min−1 to obtain the FeO0.7F1.3 sample. The as-prepared FeO0.7F1.3 sample contains a dominant phase of FeO0.77F1.23 and a minor phase of FeF3 at the molar percentages of 85.51% and 14.49%, respectively25.

Electrolyte preparation
AlCl3 (>98.0%) and tris(pentafluorophenyl)borane (TPFPB, >98.0%) were bought from Tokyo Chemical Industry Co. Ltd. Tetrahydrofuran (THF, ≥99.8%) was acquired from Alfa Aesar. Phenylmagnesium chloride (PhMgCl, ≥99.8%) and LiCl (≥99.99%) were purchased from Aladdin Reagent Co. The baseline all phenyl complex (APC)-type electrolyte was synthesized by reacting 0.25 M AlCl3 and 0.5 M PhMgCl and adding 1.0 M LiCl in THF. Specifically, 0.1333 g of AlCl3 was dissolved in 3 mL of THF with stirring overnight, and then 1 mL PhMgCl (2.0 M in THF) was added into the above solution. After the sufficient Lewis acid-base reactions, 0.1696 g LiCl was added into the solution and continuously stirred until it was completely dissolved prior to use (denoted as LiCl-APC). The additive-containing electrolyte was obtained by dissolving 0.02 M or 0.05 M TPFPB into the above LiCl-APC solution. Among them, the optimal formulation with 0.02 M TPFPB is denoted as LiCl-APC-TPFPB and used for a comparative study with the baseline LiCl-APC. All the electrolytes were prepared inside an Ar-filled glove box with oxygen and moisture contents lower than 0.1 ppm at a room temperature of 25 °C.

Electrochemical measurement
The electrochemical performance was investigated by using CR2032 coin-type cells with the as-synthesized oxyfluoride as positive electrode and the high-purity magnesium foil (Hefei KE JING Materials Technology Co., LTD., 99.95%, 50 μm in thickness) as negative electrode. The positive electrode was prepared by homogeneously mixing the FeO0.7F1.3 powder, Super P carbon (Shenzhen Kejing Zhida Technology Co., Ltd.) and poly(vinyldifluoride) (PVDF, Sigma Aldrich, Mw = ~534,000) binder with a weight ratio of 8:1:1 in the N-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., AR) solvent, followed by pasting the slurry on the 8-mm-diameter carbon paper (Toray, TGP-H-060, which was attached on a Mo current collector) and drying in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 20 h to remove the solvent. The prepared positive electrode contains the active fluoride material with a mass loading of about 1.0 mg cm−2 and has a thickness of about 24 μm. The negative-to-positive electrode capacity ratio (N/P ratio) is estimated to be about 63.6. A glass microfiber membrane (Whatman GF/B, cat. No. 1821-090, thickness=0.68 mm, average pore size=1.0 μm) with a diameter of 19 mm was employed as the separator. The APC-type solutions with and without TPFPB additive were used as the electrolytes. The volume of electrolyte injected in each coin cell is controlled at about 90 μl by pipette. The whole cell assembly process was carried out in an Ar-filled glove box.

Regular galvanostatic charge-discharge tests were operated at room temperature (25 °C, if not specially indicated) on a LAND-CT2001A battery system at various specific currents from 100 to 1000 mA g-1. The charge cut-off potential is set at 2.5, 2.7, or 3.0 V vs. Mg2+/Mg. The discharge cut-off potential is set at 1.1 V for intercalation reaction or at 0.5 V for additional conversion reaction. The cell for low temperature test was pre-cycled at 25 °C for 5 cycles and then transferred to an environment of –20 °C to conduct the following electrochemical cycling at a specific current of 20 mA g−1 in a voltage range of 0.5-3.0 V. GITT was operated at 25 °C and a low specific current of 20 mA g−1 for 1 h followed by open-circuit relaxation for 6 h to reach a quasi-equilibrium state. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), Tafel analysis, and in-situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were performed on an electrochemical workstation (VersaSTAT3, AMETEK Scientific Instruments) at 25 °C. CV measurements of Mg||FeO0.7F1.3 cells were run at different scan rates from 0.1 to 1.0 mV s−1 in various voltage ranges of 0.5–2.5 V, 0.5–2.7 V, and 0.5–3.0 V. To evaluate the oxidation stability of APC-type electrolytes and their anodic corrosion on metallic current collectors, LSV tests were conducted at a scan rate of 0.1 mV s−1 using a two-electrode or three-electrode configuration. Stainless steel (SS) or Mo foil was used as the working electrode, and Mg foils serve as the counter electrode for two-electrode configuration and as both the reference electrode and counter electrode for three-electrode configuration, respectively. The reversibility of Mg plating/stripping process in APC-type electrolytes was evaluated by conducting the galvanostatic cycling in Mg||Cu asymmetric cells at a current density of 0.5 mA cm−2 and an areal capacity of 1.0 mAh cm−2. The Cu foil (99.9%) with a thickness of 12 μm was acquired from Hefei KE JING Materials Technology Co., LTD. Tafel analysis was performed on the 10th discharge process by holding the voltage at the conversion plateau of 1.20 V for 1 h, followed by a linear scan at 1.0 mV s−1 within the voltage range of ±100 mV around the open-circuit voltage. For in-situ EIS measurements, the Mg||FeO0.7F1.3 cell was pre-cycled for 10 cycles at 100 mA g−1 in a voltage range of 0.5–3.0 V to allow the electrodes and related interfaces to reach a quasi-stable state. Then, the cell intermittently proceeded with a galvanostatic discharge-charge cycle at 100 mA g−1 in a voltage range of 0.5–3.0 V, with a specific capacity interval of 35 mAh g−1, followed by an open-circuit operation for 30 min and a potentiostatic EIS measurement to record the Nyquist plots. Each potentiostatic EIS measurement was conducted under the open-circuit condition with an applied amplitude of 10 mV, in a frequency range from 100 kHz to 1.0 Hz (12 points per decade). The obtained Nyquist plots are deconvolved for the DRT analysis using pyDRTtools software58.

Material characterization
Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy were performed to identify the effect of TPFPB mediation on the composition and solvation structure of APC-type electrolytes. The 11B and 7Li NMR spectra were collected on a Bruker Avance III HD 400 MHz spectrometer. Raman spectra were measured with a Renishaw inVia Reflex confocal Raman microscope using a 633 nm laser. The ionic conductivities of baseline APC-type electrolyte and TPFPB-containing electrolyte were measured by a DDSJ-308A conductivity meter (Leici) at 25 °C. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Magellan 400L, FEI) was employed to observe the morphology of pristine FeO0.7F1.3 grains. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL JSM-6700F, operated at 200 kV) was carried out to collect the (high-resolution) TEM images and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns, which are used to disclose the morphology and microstructure of oxyfluoride positive electrodes at terminal discharged and charged states. The (sub)surface composition and bonding evolutions of cycled FeO0.7F1.3 electrodes were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCAlab-250) with an Al anode source. For the ex-situ TEM and XPS characterizations, the discharged or charged FeO0.7F1.3 electrode was cycled at 100 mA g−1 and 25 °C for 5 cycles, and then taken out from the cells in an Ar-filled glove box. Subsequently, the collected electrodes were repeatedly washed by THF solvent to ensure the removal of residual salts. They were then dried overnight in an argon atmosphere before further characterization.

Computational details
Quantum chemical calculations were carried out using the Gaussian 09 (Revision D.01)59 software package based on density functional theory (DFT) method. The geometry optimization and single-point energy calculation were performed at the B3LYP60/6-311+G(d,p)61//M062X62/def2TZVP63 level of theory. The electrostatic potential (ESP) mapping of molecular surface with ESP surface extrema was obtained using Multiwfn (version 3.8) software64 and Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD, version 1.9.4a53) program65 based on the above single-point energy calculation. Supplementary Data 1-6 provide the optimized configurations of THF solvent and Cl− and AlCl4− anions individually, as well as their respective optimized configurations when interacting with TPFPB. The desolvation energy profiles of solvated clusters for Mg2+-ion and Li+-ion were calculated based on the paths involving sequential solvent detachment and anion dissociation. The energy barrier (E desol:) of stepwise desolvation was calculated by the following equation:

E desol: = E solvent=ion + E res: − E tot: (3)

where E solvent=ion, E res:, and E tot: represent the energies of stripped species (THF solvent, Cl⁻, or [TPFPB-Cl]⁻), residual stable configuration after stripping, and initial stable configuration before desolvation step, respectively. Supplementary Data 7–10 provide the initial and final configurations of the solvated clusters for the hexa-coordinated Mg2+(THF)5Cl⁻ and tetra-coordinated Li+(THF)3Cl− with and without TPFPB mediation during structure optimization.

The structural relaxation of FeOF and Li0.5FeOF was performed by DFT calculation using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP, version 5.3.3) with Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof parametrization of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA). The projector-augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials (version 5.2) were implemented in VASP to describe the electron-ion interaction. The PAW pseudopotentials and valence configurations for each atom used in DFT calculations are: Mg_pv(2p63s2) for magnesium, Li_sv(1s22s1) for lithium, Fe_pv(3p63d74s1) for iron, O(2s22p4) for oxygen, and F(2s22p5) for fluorine. Considering the strong correlation character of Fe 3d electrons, a Hubbard-type correction (GGA+U) with a Ueff value of 5.0 eV was applied66. A gamma-centered k-points mesh of 5×5×5 was used to sample the Brillouin zone for both FeOF and Li0.5FeOF. The activation barrier and migration pathway for charge-carrier (Mg2+ or Li+) hopping were estimated by the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method67. The potential migration pathways were constructed using the linear interpolation between initial and final states, and the structures were then relaxed with a maximum residual force threshold of 0.05 eV Å−1 for each atom. The cutoff energy was set to 450 eV, and the energy convergence criteria for structure relaxation were less than 10−6 eV. The force convergence criterion was set as 0.02 eV Å−1 for the structural relaxation of initial FeOF and Li0.5FeOF. The energy convergence criterion was less than 10−6 eV for both structure relaxations and CI-NEB calculations. The cutoff energy was set to 450 eV in all the calculations. The crystal structures of FeOF and Li0.5FeOF are obtained from Material Project68 and re-constructed according to the previous study48 using VESTA software (version 3.4.0)69. The crystal structures, clusters and differential charge density maps are visualized using VESTA software69. The schematic illustrations of the regulating effect of TPFPB on electrolyte and the reaction mechanism of FeOF co-driven by Li/Mg-ions, as well as the format backgrounds of electrochemical performance diagrams, are generated using PowerPoint software. Supplementary Data 11, 12 provide the optimized structures of FeOF and Li0.5FeOF with Mg-ion intercalation.

### Reviewer 3

In the manuscript, the authors proposed a novel Mg-fluoride battery prototype. The introduction of anion receptors into electrolyte enhances the oxidative stability and modulates the solvation structure, enabling Mg-fluoride batteries with satisfactory electrochemical performance. The conversion reaction mechanism involving dual-cation co-participation in fluorides is elucidated in depth using a combination of DFT calculations and solid characterizations. This work achieves an advance in expanding the cathode options for Mg-based batteries to high-energy fluoride cathodes. The beneficial role of anion receptors in mitigating the interfacial issues of chloride-containing electrolytes is also an interesting finding. Overall, the publication in Nature Communications is recommended after some minor issues are addressed.
(1) The magnesium chloride cations are thermodynamically stable due to the high scission energy. It is interesting to find that the Cl-related interfacial reaction activity is suppressed while enabling Mg participation in cathode reactions. Please give a detailed explanation about this phenomenon.
(2) After introducing the TPFPB additive, the APC electrolyte has demonstrated an extended electrochemical window and enhanced corrosion resistance. Is there a supportive explanation or other proof for this point?
(3) For the electrochemical performance in Figure 3, why does the Mg full cell exhibit the better cycling stability and higher CE at a low temperature of –20 °C compared to at room temperature?
(4) The activation barriers for cation diffusion in rutile-structured FeOF vary significantly along different paths. Anion coordination environment should play a critical role, meriting further explanation to clarify its impact.
(5) According to the DRT results, the charge-transfer-related peaks within a timescale range of 10-2–1 s show the distinct evolution behaviors during the charge and discharge processes. This appears to suggest distinct reaction mechanisms. Please discuss the possible underlying reasons.

### Reviewer 5

Chen et al. reported the oxyfluoride FeO0.7F1.3 as a cathode material for magnesium metal batteries, and employed a TPFPB-mediated electrolyte to mitigate interfacial side reactions, thereby achieving stable high-voltage operation. The TPFPB-mediated solvation environment reduces the desolvation energy barrier, further contributing to high-capacity and low-temperature-tolerant Mg-FeO0.7F1.3 cells. The development of fluoride-based magnesium batteries is novel and may be of great value. The electrochemical performance is impressive, and the underlying understanding of the reaction mechanism is provided. I consider that a minor revision is necessary before the acceptance of this manuscript. My specific comments are listed below.
1. The authors performed detailed DFT calculations to analyze the regulation effect of TPFPB on cation solvation structures. However, the related regulation mechanism requires further clarification. Additionally, experimental evidence supporting the change in solvation environment should be provided.
2. Figure 1e shows a significant improvement in electrolyte oxidation stability upon TPFPB addition. The authors ascribe this to altered chemical components in the electrolyte. They are suggested to explain clearly how TPFPB affect the electrolyte oxidation stability by changing the chemical components.
3. The intercalation-type cells exhibit the divergence in Coulombic efficiency during the later stages of long-term cycling. What might be the potential causes of this behavior?
4. Regarding the dual-cation co-driven reaction mechanism, whether Mg2+ ions or MgCl+ species are involved in the cathode reactions?
5. Why is the ion migration kinetics enhanced in the FeOF structure following partial lithiation reaction?
6. Does the acceptor additive participate in the formation of the CEI layer observed in the TEM images?

Response to "The stoichiometry of FeO F (0 ≤ x ≤ 1) with x=0.7 implies an odd assortment of Fe O phases in addition to FeF that are potentially inactive":
We propose the reaction mechanism of iron oxyfluoride driven by dual-cationic charge carriers in Fig. 5I (as seen below), which also reveals the role of oxygen component in the reversible cycle of oxyfluoride cathode. The discharge process enables the solid-solution-like electrochemical lithiation, followed by the Li+/Mg2+ co-driven conversion reactions that result in the retained RS-phase Li FeO and extruded Fe metal, LiF and MgF (in the confined voltage). The cubic lattice coherence and similar lattice constants of these discharge products tend to promote the local electronic and ionic transport at multiphase interfaces. It has a positive effect on the reinjection of Fe/F components into Li FeO upon the delithiation/demagnesiation (charge) process, thus being advantageous to reconstitute the parent structure and maintain the particle integrity. Therefore, although the Fe O moiety in iron oxyfluorides is not fully activated (i.e., it does not participate in the conversion reaction), the retained Li FeO intermediate could serve as a favorable substrate structure to promote the reconstitution of parent oxyfluoride structure. Compared with the FeF cathode, which undergoes the deep phase transformation during conversion reaction, the FeO F cathodes typically deliver the higher kinetic capacity at the expense of thermodynamic capacity based on the partial conversion reaction mode.
On the other hand, the oxygen/fluorine substitution in rutile-type FeF enables the solid solution form of FeII FeIII O F (0 ≤ x ≤ 1), indicating that oxygen (1~x) x x 2~x doping will increase the valence state of Fe and boost the theoretical capacity for oxyfluorides (from 571 mAh g-1 for FeF to 884 mAh g-1 for FeOF). The increased Fe3+ content in FeO F could enhance the intercalation reaction in high voltage region. Overall, the introduction of oxygen into oxyfluoride cathodes facilitates their sustainable cycling with high capacity and high energy release.

Response: Thanks for the valuable suggestion! We have presented the average CE and capacity loss for the first 10 cycles of Mg-FeO F cells using LiCl-APC and LiCl-APC-TPFPB electrolytes in newly added Supplementary Figs. 17 and 18 (as seen below). For the conversion-type cells (Supplementary Fig. 17), a low average CE value of 77% is yielded in the LiCl-APC system, which should result from the severe interfacial side reactions due to the poor oxidation stability of electrolyte. Moreover, the converted metallic iron in cycled fluoride cathode is susceptible to the anodic corrosion from Cl-based electrolyte and has a potential catalytic effect on interfacial side reaction. By comparison, using the LiCl-APC-TPFPB electrolyte with enhanced anti-oxidation ability, the Mg-FeO F cells perform the higher average CE values (in a range of 87%–94%) for the first 10 cycles, even at the higher charge cut-off voltages. Benefiting from its high-voltage tolerance, the LiCl-APC-TPFPB electrolyte enables the 3.0 V class cell to achieve good cycling stability with the lowering of capacity loss to 28%, compared with 44% of capacity loss for the 2.5 V class cell using LiCl-APC electrolyte. For the intercalation-type cells, the decreased phase transformation degree and reduced volume variation can mitigate the surface activity-related side reactions of fluoride cathodes. Consequently, the Mg-FeO F cells with two APC-type electrolytes both deliver the higher levels of CE, with the TPFPB-containing systems still exhibiting the relatively higher average CE values (in a range of 91%-96%) for the first 10 cycles (Supplementary Fig. 18). A reduction in capacity loss of Mg-FeO F cells from 50% to 32% can be achieved when TPFPB is added to the APC-type electrolyte. Overall, from the performance perspective, the initial capacity loss and coulombic efficiency need to be further improved in future studies on the emerging Mg-fluoride batteries. Our study presents a promising research direction to develop electrolyte materials with a wide electrochemical window, enabling the good compatibilities with both high-potential fluoride cathodes and passivation-sensitive Mg anodes.

To reviewer #2 and reviewer #3：
In the manuscript, the authors proposed a novel Mg-fluoride battery prototype. The introduction of anion receptors into electrolyte enhances the oxidative stability and modulates the solvation structure, enabling Mg-fluoride batteries with satisfactory electrochemical performance. The conversion reaction mechanism involving dual-cation co-participation in fluorides is elucidated in depth using a combination of DFT calculations and solid characterizations. This work achieves an advance in expanding the cathode options for Mg-based batteries to high-energy fluoride cathodes. The beneficial role of anion receptors in mitigating the interfacial issues of chloride-containing electrolytes is also an interesting finding. Overall, the publication in Nature Communications is recommended after some minor issues are addressed.
Response: Thanks for the positive and insightful comments from the reviewers. We have improved our work based on the following detailed comments proposed by the reviewers.
(1) The magnesium chloride cations are thermodynamically stable due to the high scission energy. It is interesting to find that the Cl-related interfacial reaction activity is suppressed while enabling Mg participation in cathode reactions. Please give a detailed explanation about this phenomenon.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s comment. According to the quantum chemical calculations (Fig. 1A), TPFPB receptor shows the strong electrostatic attraction with magnesium chloride complexes with the binding energies of −1.06, −1.18, and −1.33 eV for MgCl+, MgCl , and Mg Cl +, respectively. Note that the absorbed Mg Cl + 2 2 3 2 3 cluster on TPFPB undergoes structural deformation (Supplementary Fig. 1), where one of the chlorine atoms breaks the original Mg-Cl-Mg bridge and approaches the boron center of anion receptor. It seems that the introduction of TPFPB is unfavorable for the stable existence of Mg Cl + species in APC solution. Driven by the 2 3 TPFPB-induced interaction, the Raman peak related to [Mg Cl ·6THF]+ becomes 2 3 somewhat blurred and shows an evident blue shift from 245 cm-1 to 252 cm-1 (Fig. 1D). This confirms the structural instability of Mg Cl + species when interacting with 2 3 TPFPB. As a major culprit for corrosion, the decreased concentration of [Mg Cl ·6THF]+ is expected to alleviate the corrosivity of 2 3 TPFPB-mediated electrolyte. On the other hand, according to the DFT calculations on ion desolvation processes (Fig. 2C), the energy barrier for rate-determining Mg2+-Cl⁻ scission is substantially lowered from 3.07 eV to 2.09 eV, and it is facilitated by the formation of thermodynamically stable [TPFPB-Cl]⁻ complex. Overall, the strong electrostatic attraction between TPFPB and chlorine ligand can promote the dechlorination process of Mg2+ cation and alleviate the Cl-related side reactions at cathode-electrolyte interface.

(4) The activation barriers for cation diffusion in rutile-structured FeOF vary significantly along different paths. Anion coordination environment should play a critical role, meriting further explanation to clarify its impact.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s valuable comment. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 27, there are three anion channels (i.e. mixed O/F, F, and O channels) along [001] direction, which provide the potential pathways (denoted as path 1, 2, and 3, respectively) for cation migration in rutile-type FeOF structure. Along the three paths, the intercalated cations can pass through the metastable octahedral sites when hopping between adjacent stable octahedral sites (Fig. 5B), which requires activation energy to overcome the corresponding energy barrier. The calculated energy barriers of path 1, 2, and 3 for Li-ion migration are 1.39, 0.18, and 4.40 eV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 27F). The highest energy barrier of path 3 should be attributed to the strong electrostatic interaction between intercalated cation and bivalent lattice O2- with concentrated charge nature. The electrostatic force also drives the Fe atoms to move off-center towards the O atoms, thereby increasing the Fe3+-Li+ repulsion in O channel due to shortened distance (Supplementary Fig. 27E). As a result, the octahedral sites for Li occupation are in off-center positions after lattice relaxation (Supplementary Fig. 27D). It can be deduced that the lithiation sites within the mixed and F channels (denoted as H1 and H2 respectively) are more energetically favorable or stable than t hose within the O channels (Fig. 5A).

Chen et al. reported the oxyfluoride FeO F as a cathode material for magnesium 0.7 1.3 metal batteries, and employed a TPFPB-mediated electrolyte to mitigate interfacial side reactions, thereby achieving stable high-voltage operation. In the APC-type solutions where Mg²⁺ and Li⁺ ions are typically coordinated by a combination of Cl- and THF ligands, we employed quantum chemistry simulations to optimize the solvated configurations of both Mg-ion (i.e. Mg2+(THF)ₙCl⁻) and Li-ion (i.e. Li+(THF)ₙCl⁻), systematically comparing the cases with and without TPFPB mediation (Supplementary Figs. 6-9). As shown in Fig. 2B, the introduction of TPFPB extends the Mg···Cl distance between Mg2+ and Cl- as well as the average Mg···O distance between Mg2+ and THF for Mg solvation complexes. Similar trends are seen for the Li solvation complexes in terms of Li···Cl and Li···O coordination distances (Fig. 2C).

As a major culprit for corrosion, the decreased concentration of [Mg Cl ·6THF]+ is expected to alleviate the corrosivity of 2 3 TPFPB-mediated electrolyte. 3. The intercalation-type cells exhibit the divergence in Coulombic efficiency during the later stages of long-term cycling. What might be the potential causes of this behavior?
Response: As shown in Supplementary Fig. 13, the initial discharge profile displays the sole solid solution reaction stage without involving the conversion reaction, offering a dominant plateau at ~1.75 V with a capacity beyond 200 mAh g-1. As the cycling proceeds, the cell with LiCl-APC electrolyte suffers from the evident plateau degradation and capacity decrease. Note that the second-stage discharge plateau appears at below ~1.5 V after 200 cycles (Supplementary Fig. 13A), indicating the occurrence of conversion reaction in fluoride cathode. The accumulation of converted metallic Fe is prone to induce anodic corrosion and parasitic side reactions, which should be responsible for the sharp CE decline in subsequent cycling (Fig. 3F). In comparison, the modified cell with TPFPB addition can well maintain the sloped intercalation plateau within 300 cycles without involving conversion reaction (Supplementary Fig. 13B).

4. Regarding the dual-cation co-driven reaction mechanism, whether Mg2+ ions or MgCl+ species are involved in the cathode reactions?
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s comment. From the XPS concentration-depth profiles of the discharged FeO F cathode (Supplementary Fig. 26), the atomic 0.7 1.3 fractions of Cl and Al elements show a descending trend with etching, which is different from those of the active elements such as Fe, F, Li, and Mg. Correspondingly, the Mg-F and Mg-Cl components show the opposite concentration evolutions from surface to subsurface, according to the increased peak area for Mg-F and decreased peak area for Mg-Cl in Mg 1s spectra (Supplementary Fig. 25D). It can be deduced that the detected Cl-based species are mainly residual chloride salts covering the cathode surface and are not deeply involved in fluoride reactions. Consequently, due to the dechlorination effect of TPFPB, the magnesiation reactions of fluoride cathode should be mainly dominated by Mg2+ ions rather than MgCl+ species.

5. Why is the ion migration kinetics enhanced in the FeOF structure following partial lithiation reaction?
Response: Based on the reviewer’s suggestion, we first analyzed the DFT-relaxed structures of FeOF and Li FeOF. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 29, it causes the 0.5 obvious lattice expansion along b-axis with the elongation of Fe-F and Fe-O bonds from FeOF to Li FeOF. Notably, the volume of octahedral site for further cation 0.5 occupation along the empty mixed O/F channel correspondingly increases by 29%. On the other hand, the Li-cation pre-intercalation also has an impact on the electron redistribution upon subsequent Mg insertion in Li FeOF. The differential 0.5 charge density of Mg-ion intercalated in FeOF (Fig. 5C) shows a pronounced charge transfer from divalent Mg-ion to FeOF host, leading to the formation of charge depletion zone around Mg and charge accumulation region around adjacent O and F atoms. This explains why the migration kinetics of Mg-ions in FeOF structure is sluggish (Fig. 5D). As for Li FeOF, the charge accumulation on O/F ligands 0.5 near Mg ion is markedly reduced (Fig. 5G), implying the weakened interaction between intercalated Mg-ion and Li FeOF host. Overall, the expanded channel 0.5 spacing and weakened electrostatic interaction are expected to enhance the cation mobility along mixed O/F path (Fig. 5F), lowering the migration energy barriers to 0.50 eV for Li-ions and to 2.32 eV for Mg-ions (Fig. 5H).
